extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians, historians and philosophers of mathematics, and advanced students interested in the methodology of proofs and concept-formation
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for analysing and forming mathematical conjectures, proofs and definitions — especially how to treat counterexamples, hidden lemmas, and how proofs reshape concepts. Focuses on methodology rather than specific formal results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish logical vs heuristic counterexamples
rubrics_metrics.description: Classify counterexamples as 'logical' (global but not local) or 'heuristic' (local but not global), and also recognise counterexamples that are both global and local; treat heuristic/global-local distinctions as relevant to whether a case is merely logically problematic or actually informative for content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text: 'We may call the first (global but not local) counterexamples logical, the others heuristic counterexamples.' Heuristic counterexamples (and those that are both global and local) are important because they reveal poverty of content and stimulate the growth of knowledge — e.g. picture-frames serve as both global and local counterexamples to Cauchy's theorem: corroborative for truth alone but refutational for content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use counterexamples to drive conceptual change
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat counterexamples not merely as failures to be patched but as stimuli that indicate which lemmas, assumptions or concepts need rethinking and which new theoretical distinctions should be introduced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The more refutations you recognise (logical or heuristic), the quicker knowledge grows. Counterexamples can reveal hidden false 'obvious' lemmas that should be made explicit or can motivate new proof-generated concepts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make hidden lemmas explicit (lemma-incorporation)
rubrics_metrics.description: When a proof appears to rely on tacit assumptions, these hidden lemmas should be identified and incorporated into the explicit formulation of the theorem rather than being silently assumed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrary to the intuition that adding lemmas contracts content, the text argues lemma-incorporation increases content: making hidden premises explicit can generalise the theorem and create proof-generated concepts (example: turning the vague 'polyhedron' into 'Cauchy-objects').

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish monster-barring from concept-stretching (monster-including)
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognise two opposing responses to counterexamples: monster-barring (excluding problematic examples by narrowing the definition) and concept-stretching (including previously 'monstrous' examples by widening the concept); these have different epistemic effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Monster-barring often merely translates or preserves the original naive concept; concept-stretching expands the conceptual space and can expose richer theory. Beware of accusing opponents of 'surreptitious' contractions when, historically, refutationists were often the ones expanding concepts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pin down intended interpretation vs unintended wide definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Be explicit about the intended interpretation of terms and check that formal definitions actually capture that intention; naive or casually stated definitions can unintentionally be much wider and mislead debate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Legendre's plausible Definition 1 ('A polyhedron is a solid whose surface consists of polygonal faces') covered far more than intended, allowing refutationists to exploit it. Authors should make tacit clauses explicit to avoid unintended broadening.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow proof-methods to generate concepts (proof-generated/theory-generated classification)
rubrics_metrics.description: Accept that different proofs may yield different 'proof-generated' concepts and that these new theoretical classifications can legitimately replace naive ones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A proof's allowable operations (stretching, pumping, projecting, photographing) determine a class of objects for which the theorem holds. e.g., 'Cauchy-objects' (objects on which Cauchy's proof can be performed) may include curvilinear or 'pumped' polyhedra that the naive concept did not encompass.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognise that deduction must increase content (avoid sterile verification)
rubrics_metrics.description: A genuine deduction should increase content (i.e., produce non-trivial new consequences); if a purported 'deduction' does not increase content, it is mere verification and epistemically sterile.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quotation from text: 'verification differs from true demonstration precisely because it is purely analytic and because it is sterile.' Thus insist that proofs expand theoretical content rather than just rephrase premises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be cautious about ad hoc redefinitions to save a theorem
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid rescuing a theorem by making surreptitious, ad hoc adjustments to definitions that hide the real problem; such terminological epicycles are intellectually dubious unless properly justified and made explicit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text criticises attempts like Hoppe's 'monster-adjustment' (counting common vertices/edges twice or re-labelling pieces) as hiding problems rather than confronting them. If a definition changes, state and justify it clearly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formulate theorems in proof-generated language when appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: When a proof determines the effective domain of a theorem, state the theorem in terms of proof-generated objects (e.g., 'All Cauchy-objects are Eulerian') rather than in naive terms that have lost their original meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This prevents confusion between naive historical intentions and the new class of objects for which the proof actually supplies an explanation; it makes explicit the connection between method and scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accept that proofs can erase naive problems and produce new questions
rubrics_metrics.description: Understand that a successful proof may dissolve the original naive problem (its central concepts) and replace it with new, theory-generated problems and concepts; this is part of scientific/mathematical progress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The naive notion (e.g., of 'polyhedron' as a crystal-like solid) can disappear under proof-analysis; what remains are the proof-generated notions (stretchability, projectability, etc.) and new research problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: When generalising formulae (e.g., Euler characteristic), identify the correct combinatorial/topological contributors
rubrics_metrics.description: Generalisations of classical formulae must identify which structural features affect the invariant (e.g., ringshaped faces vs 'inner polygons', cavities, multiply-connected components), not rely on naive counts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text presents corrected generalisations for Euler characteristic: e.g., for normal n-spheroid polyhedra V - E + F = 2 - 2(n - 1); for multiply-connected faces one must add sum ek (contributions from ringshaped faces); earlier attempts (Lhuilier) that counted 'inner polygons' or mis-handled tunnels/cavities were incomplete. Beware multiply-connected cavities, branching tunnels, and ambiguity in counting tunnels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate historical claims cautiously (avoid retroactive rationalisation of intentions)
rubrics_metrics.description: When assessing historical proofs or theorems, don't assume original authors had modern conceptual frameworks; be wary of attributing to past mathematicians explicit restrictions or intentions that they did not state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text critiques historians who 'save' Cauchy by claiming he must have tacitly restricted his theorem to convex polyhedra. Instead, historical actors often operated within narrower conceptual frameworks and their proofs generated later generalisations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer enlarging conceptual frameworks over protecting naive certainty
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid valuing apparent certainty that arises from narrow, unimagined frameworks; conceptual poverty and lack of imagination can produce false comfort, while recognising and responding to counterexamples fosters theory growth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The example given: a theorist who takes 'all polyhedra are simple' as obvious will not be stimulated by counterexamples to clarify lemmas and thus will miss opportunities for generating deeper theory.
